events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Cheekface is an indie rock trio, more precisely a talk-singing band, from Los Angeles. The story starts in 2017. Things were getting pretty crappy on Earth. Indie rock lifers Greg and Mandy got together to write out the anxiety, despair and the bleak humor of it all. They sent the demos to Echo and, voila, a band. It wasn't a project that started with much ambition: the idea was to drop a record on Bandcamp and call it a day. But in 2018, the band's second single "Dry Heat/Nice Town," a playful pub rock tune about leftist protest culture, started to snowball online. A word-of-mouth cult started to form, and it intensified with Cheekface's community-minded singalong shows. Fans dubbed themselves "Cheek Freaks." The band chased their 2019 debut LP "Therapy Island" with 2021's "Emphatically No," which bowed as Bandcamp's top-selling alternative album. Their 3rd LP "Too Much to Ask" in 2022 was a watershed moment: it shot to \#2 on the non-commercial radio chart, and The Needle Drop proclaimed it one of the year's best albums. Cheekface's 4th album "It's Sorted" came out January 22, 2024. Touring to support "It's Sorted," the band sold out shows across the US, Canada and the UK. The band self-released their 5th long player “Middle Spoon” in February 2025.

events.summary: Run Time: 180 min. TICKETS $15 Doors & interactive synth experience at 6:30 p.m.; Event 7 p.m. The film will start after !mindparade's performance. Select Showtime to Purchase Tickets Click here to learn more about accessibility at the Tomorrow Theater. THE EXPERIENCE The Portland Synth Library co-presents a one-of-a-kind documentary about pioneering American composer, teacher, and Deep Listening founder Pauline Oliveros. Before the film, in honor of Pauline, a modular synth for drones and field recordings will be on hand courtesy of the synth library for individuals to try out. This will be followed by a visual and audio treat from the band !mindparade before moving into director Daniel Weintraub's fascinating documentary Deep Listening: The Story of Pauline Oliveros. ON SCREEN: Deep Listening: The Story of Pauline Oliveros 2022. Directed by Daniel Weintraub. Runtime: 117 minutes. Deep Listening: The Story of Pauline Oliveros tells the story of the iconic composer, performer, teacher, philosopher, technological innovator, and humanitarian, Pauline Oliveros. She was one of the world's original electronic musicians, one of the only females amongst notable post-war American composers, a master accordion player, a teacher and mentor to musicians, a gateway to music and sound for non-musicians, and a technical innovator who helped develop everything from tools that allow musicians to play together while in different countries to software that enables those with severe disabilities to create beautiful music. On the vanguard of contemporary American music for six decades, her story illuminates the pathway to how we got where we are and where the future will take us in the worlds of music, the philosophy of sound, and the art of listening. ON STAGE: !mindparade \(musicians\) - !mindparade blends elements of art pop, psych, and experimentalism. Their music has been described as a "bedroom symphony marked by flourishing psychedelic arrangements" \(NUVO\) and "a perfect slice of what's best in Oregon Pop Music." \(Oregon Arts Watch\). The band tours its distinct sound to venues big and small, with recent appearances at festivals like Treefort Fest \(Boise\), Freakout Fest \(Seattle\), Sh'Bang Festival \(Bellingham\), and Lose Yr Mind Fest \(Portland\). They have shared the stage with acts such as Bill Callahan, Pearl and The Oysters, The Shivas, Corridor, and many more. !mindparade is based in Portland, Oregon. In 2020, the group founded their own label, Neon Underground Archives, in order to self-release their genre-bending records.Their 2026 release, "Neon Gummi Jukebox", dives into a progressive synthesizer driven genre they have dubbed "vaporprog". Synth Library Portland is a collectively-run 501\(c\)\(3\) arts non-profit providing low-cost access to electronic music gear and education, since 2016. We build community and empower people to experiment, learn, and create. At our dedicated space in Central Eastside, we offer workshops, meetups, studio access, concerts, and a gear lending program. AUDIOLOGY
events.title: Deep Listening: The Story Of Pauline Oliveros

events.summary: Strange & the Familiars have been telling tall tales to Portland audiences for seven years. These are tales about lost people with unusual abilities, dark friends from unexpected places, and warnings from the wordless. Heavily inspired by the work of literary and comic book artists, Strange & the Familiars presents an immersive musical experience that straddles the line between rock opera and musical theatre storytelling while exploring the dark and fantastical places in the human mind. They released their first album, Pretty Deadly, in 2016 (a nod to the graphic novel of the same name created by Kelly Sue DeConnick and Emma Rios), followed by a more explicit invitation into this dark and whimsical world with their sophomore release of Strange World in 2021. Between musical releases Stephanie Strange has been writing and telling stories and collaborating with visual artists in bits and bobs, as transmission quality allows. Flying Caravan through the sunrise into the sunset cloud castles with rivers of rainbows Fern Spores is a femme-folk-rock band rooted in Olympia, WA. Gracefully flowing between vintage psych folk, garage rock, clever covers, and soulful Americana ballads they curate a truly original sound. Their songs are both anthems of empowerment and poignant reflections on life’s highs and lows. Angsty but uplifting, whimsical yet fierce, and as rock as it is roll. Drawing inspiration from musical legends like Janis Joplin, Susan Tedeschi, and The Runaways, they infuse vintage tones with modern perspective. Fern Spores is an all woman band fronted by singer-songwriters Alyssa Nunke and Jade Kovats. Their full band arrangement includes Abbey Ryle (fiddle), and Katie Welch (drums). Their debut album, The Understory, released in 2024 and they are currently working on their second album, The Thicket. They’ve performed over 200 shows across 5 states since forming in 2023.
events.title: Strange & the Familiars w/ Flying Caravan and Fern Spores

We'll anchor much of our work in the teachings & approaches of Augusto Boal and Paulo Friere, two educators who helped bring this style of improvisation to the world. Together, we'll learn how to: 🗣️ Share our most powerful life stories with honesty & vulnerability 💥 Explore those stories with creativity & support 👁️ See & experience our lives through the lens of others 💪🏼 Discover our psychological strengths and, most importantly... ❤️ Evolve our relationships through the power of insight 🗣️ 1:1 Sessions Included The practice of applied improvisation is fun, but also requires vulnerability. events.summary: TICKETS ️ truewest.info/Cooke26 On Sale Now! ---------------------------------------- She Wants Revenge, the dark-alternative duo who first exploded onto the scene with the 2005 hit, “Tear You Apart”, are back with a new song, festival appearances, a new lineup, and a massive global audience hungry for the 3rd wave gothic rock they ushered in 2up and down decades before. For Justin Warfield and Adam Bravin, She Wants Revenge began as a production duo making songs to DJ at clubs. But when a 3-song demo was passed to a friend, they signed to Geffen records, and soon the songs became the basis of their 2005 self-titled LP. They hit the road supporting Bloc Party, The Kills, and OKGO, and along the way, “Tear You Apart” became a bona fide hit. Soon they were opening for Depeche Mode, The Psychedelic Furs, Placebo, co-headlining with Peter Murphy of Bauhaus, headlining Coachella alongside Daft Punk, and in constant rotation on alternative rock across the country. In under a year the oddball tune they thought to be an evil cousin of the B52’s and Wall of Voodoo saw them blitzing through the late-night talk show circuit, and with singles “Out of Control”, and “These Things” also climbing the charts, they went on to sell over 300,000 albums. Though they came to prominence in the mid-aughts post-punk revival, Justin and Adam were more indebted to their early influences; Prince, Tangerine Dream, ELO, Giorgio Moroder, and 90s hip-hop. It was their true to the era production style, thoughtful songwriting, and heart-on-the-sleeve lyricism which ran counter to the studied dance punk and emotionally distanced, clever sound of their contemporaries which endeared them to the legions of fans who hungered for their brand of bold, emotive music which was sorely lacking at the time. In doing so, they made fans of both the older “all-black” crowd as well as their younger counterparts, and more pointedly, drew nods and praise from the bands who directly inspired them - cementing SWR’s legacy as torch bearers for the moody and morose who came before. Now, with a revamped lineup featuring Justin on vocals/guitar, Adam on Bass VI and synths,Thomas Froggatt \(formerly guitar\) on bass, Tony Bevilacqua \(The Distillers\) on guitar, and Lia Braswell \(Sextile, A Place To Bury Strangers, TR/ST\) on drums, the revitalized SWR exudes the same sort of spirit they first hit the road with 20 years ago. With prominent slots at their beloved hometown Cruel World festival, the UK’s sister fest Forever Now, plans for the Summer and into next year, a new song in the wings, and recording of the long-teased 4th LP still underway, She Wants Revenge is doing what would seem impossible for bands of their era - staying true to the dark dance music and gothic sound they first pioneered decades past, while also remaining fresh, reinventing, and playing music with joy to the millions of kids getting to experience it for the first time

events.summary: Flor de Toloache arrives at The Reser on October 15 with a performance that celebrates the evolution, passion, and power of mariachi music. As New York City's first and only all-female mariachi group, Flor de Toloache has become an international sensation, redefining the genre through a vibrant fusion of traditional mariachi with jazz, rock, pop, and R&B influences. Founded in 2008 by Mireya I. Ramos and Shae Fiol, the ensemble is known for its extraordinary musicianship, emotional performances, and multicultural identity, with members representing Mexico, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Cuba, Colombia, Germany, Italy, and the United States. Their innovative artistry has earned them worldwide acclaim, including the 2017 Latin Grammy Award for Best Ranchero/Mariachi Album for Las Caras Lindas. The honor recognized not only the group's exceptional talent, but also its groundbreaking role in expanding the boundaries of mariachi while remaining deeply rooted in tradition. Flor de Toloache has shared stages with acclaimed artists including Natalia Lafourcade, John Legend, and Mon Laferte, and has appeared at iconic festivals and venues such as Coachella and the Ryman Auditorium. Their performance at The Reser promises an unforgettable evening of musical excellence, cultural celebration, and artistic innovation that bridges generations and musical traditions alike.
events.title: The Reser Presents: Flor de Toloache

events.summary: Our audiences have been asking us to bring back the Halloween show for years…. Be careful what you wish for. Stephen Mallatratt’s The Woman in Black has been terrifying audiences since its London debut in 1987 and is one of the most successful and terrifying shows in West End history. Based on Susan Hill’s beloved novel, it’s one of the most celebrated ghost stories ever staged: atmospheric, relentless, and the kind of theatrical experience that makes you question every shadow on your way to the car. Set in a remote English village, it follows a young lawyer unraveling the secrets of a recently deceased client and the vengeful presence that doesn’t want him to. Just two actors portray all the characters, leaning into what B&B’s performers do best. Chilling, clever, and unforgettable. Halloween is back at Bag&Baggage…and we brought something with us. Show Dates: October 15 – November 1, 2026 Thu – Sat at 7:30pm, Sun at 2pm Special Dates: Thursday, October 15 is a preview performance, with discounted tickets. Friday, October 16, is Opening Night! Sat, Oct. 24th – ASL Interpreted Performance Sun, Oct. 25th – Audio Described Performance
events.title: The Woman In Black

events.summary: "Marigolds y Memorias" is an original devised production inspired by the traveling carpa tradition, in which humor, music, and storytelling come together in a vibrant theatrical journey. Guided by an elder, a younger generation learns to build an altar, the heart of Día de Muertos, discovering the meaning behind each of its elements, from candles and marigolds to photographs, ofrendas, and cherished recuerdos. Through song, dance, and short theatrical vignettes, the altar gradually takes shape as an act of remembrance and cultural inheritance, inviting audiences to consider how traditions are taught, how memory is kept alive, and what is carried forward when we share rituals across generations. Age Recommendation: All Ages Estimated Running Time: 1 hour 30 minutes, including one intermission
events.title: Marigolds y Memorias

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.
events.title: You Can't Take It With You

events.summary: Glass. Kill. Bluebeard. Imp. is a collection of four short, surreal plays by acclaimed English playwright, Caryl Churchill. Premiering at London's Royal Court Theatre in 2019, these darkly imaginative works weave together myth, fairy tale, and contemporary horror. Moving between collective voices and intimate encounters, Churchill explores violence, power, desire, and the stories we tell to make sense of a fractured world. By turns funny, haunting, and unsettling, the plays invite audiences into a landscape where the familiar becomes strange and ancient myths reveal modern anxieties without explanation or comfort. A girl made of glass. Gods and murders. A serial killer's friends. And a secret in a bottle.​ Four short plays by Caryl Churchill Directed by Samantha Van Der Merwe​October 10th - November 7th 2026
events.title: Glass. Kill. Bluebeard. Imp. by Caryl Churchill

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: Lookout Landscape is an immersive art exhibition by Oregon-based artist and designer David Buckley Borden and a team of collaborators working across forestry, design, and engineering. Inspired by fire lookout towers, trail culture, and backcountry gear, the exhibition invites visitors onto a fabricated “Lookout Trail,” where a series of imaginative scenes—from a trailhead to a weather station, campground, and tool shed—reimagine the visual language of forestry and outdoor culture in the Pacific Northwest. Blending research, humor, and design, the exhibition explores the complex relationships between people and working forests, with wildfire as an underlying thread. As visitors move through the space, they are encouraged to reflect on how forests are shaped, valued, and cared for, and to consider their own connection to these landscapes. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

Images that capture the fun and nostalgia of playing in a scary space through a safe lens, reminiscent of horror movies and Halloweens past. events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: From an early age, Booker T. Jones-"one of the legends of soul music" \(The New Yorker\)-was captivated by the magic of melody, rhythm, and harmony. So magnetic was the attraction, in fact, that by the time he turned sixteen, he was, incredibly, already a working musician with a hit song to his name. As part of the first house band for Stax Records, he formed the category-defining group Booker T. & the MGs, whose first recording, "Green Onions," was an international sensation, selling more than one million copies and winning a place among Rolling Stone's top five hundred songs of all time. Not stopping there, Jones continued to push soul music's boundaries, refining it to its essence and then injecting it into the nation's bloodstream. From midcentury Memphis, where the brutality of segregation was a stark backdrop to the loving, supportive family and community in which he was raised, to the creative hotbed of Beale Street, the Harlem of the South; from his early friendship with figures such as Maurice White \(who went on to form Earth, Wind, and Fire\) to the complicated dynamics of the racially mixed MGs-Jones not only was a witness to revolutions but also wrote their soundtracks. His musical legacy includes enduring compositions such as "Time Is Tight," "Hip Hug-Her," and the often sampled "Melting Pot" and collaborations with the likes of Otis Redding, Wilson Pickett, and Sam and Dave-and later Neil Young, Bob Dylan, Barbra Streisand, Carlos Santana, and Willie Nelson. Nearly five decades later, Jones's influence continues to help define the music industry, but only now is he ready to tell his remarkable life story. Time is Tight is the deeply moving account of how Jones balanced the brutality of the segregationist South with the loving support of his family and community, all while transforming a burgeoning studio into a musical mecca. Booker T. Jones is an American multi-instrumentalist, songwriter, record producer, and arranger. Best known as the front man of the band Booker T. & the MGs, he has worked with countless award-winning artists of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries and has earned a Grammy Award for Lifetime Achievement. Along with the band, he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1992. Jones continues to record and tour internationally, both as a solo artist and as head of Booker T.'s Stax Revue. events.summary: Abaraz ⴰⴱⴰⵔⴰⵣ Gateway to the Sahara Lamiae Naki was born in Fes and grew up hearing the music of Mhamid El Ghizlane, a small oasis town at the edge of the Moroccan Sahara where Arab, Amazigh, West African, and Saharan traditions have crossed paths for centuries. Climate change and migration are reshaping the region, and with it, these traditions. Naki, whose family roots are in Southern Morocco, traveled there with Seffarine co-founder Nat Hulskamp to record with local musicians and document the community's songs and stories. That material is at the heart of Abaraz - original compositions alongside traditional pieces, brought forward by an ensemble that spans Morocco, Spain, and the Pacific Northwest. On stage, frame drums, oud, guimbri, ngoni, flamenco percussion, and Naki's voice carry music that has traveled the same trade routes for generations. The performance weaves live music together with video projections and field recordings made in Mhamid - an enchanting portrait of a place the we don't often hear from. Abaraz is supported by grants from the Oregon Community Foundation and The James F. and Marion L. Miller Foundation, and was commissioned by the PRAx Center for the Performing Arts at Oregon State University.
events.title: The Reser Presents: Seffarine: Abaraz

events.summary: Our audiences have been asking us to bring back the Halloween show for years…. Be careful what you wish for. Stephen Mallatratt’s The Woman in Black has been terrifying audiences since its London debut in 1987 and is one of the most successful and terrifying shows in West End history. Based on Susan Hill’s beloved novel, it’s one of the most celebrated ghost stories ever staged: atmospheric, relentless, and the kind of theatrical experience that makes you question every shadow on your way to the car. Set in a remote English village, it follows a young lawyer unraveling the secrets of a recently deceased client and the vengeful presence that doesn’t want him to. Just two actors portray all the characters, leaning into what B&B’s performers do best. Chilling, clever, and unforgettable. Halloween is back at Bag&Baggage…and we brought something with us. events.summary: "Marigolds y Memorias" is an original devised production inspired by the traveling carpa tradition, in which humor, music, and storytelling come together in a vibrant theatrical journey. Guided by an elder, a younger generation learns to build an altar, the heart of Día de Muertos, discovering the meaning behind each of its elements, from candles and marigolds to photographs, ofrendas, and cherished recuerdos. Through song, dance, and short theatrical vignettes, the altar gradually takes shape as an act of remembrance and cultural inheritance, inviting audiences to consider how traditions are taught, how memory is kept alive, and what is carried forward when we share rituals across generations. Age Recommendation: All Ages Estimated Running Time: 1 hour 30 minutes, including one intermission
events.title: Marigolds y Memorias

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.
events.title: You Can't Take It With You

events.summary: Glass. Kill. Bluebeard. Imp. is a collection of four short, surreal plays by acclaimed English playwright, Caryl Churchill. Premiering at London's Royal Court Theatre in 2019, these darkly imaginative works weave together myth, fairy tale, and contemporary horror. Moving between collective voices and intimate encounters, Churchill explores violence, power, desire, and the stories we tell to make sense of a fractured world. By turns funny, haunting, and unsettling, the plays invite audiences into a landscape where the familiar becomes strange and ancient myths reveal modern anxieties without explanation or comfort. A girl made of glass. Gods and murders. A serial killer's friends. And a secret in a bottle.​ Four short plays by Caryl Churchill Directed by Samantha Van Der Merwe​October 10th - November 7th 2026
events.title: Glass. Kill. Bluebeard. Imp. by Caryl Churchill

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

events.summary: In the waning days of 2024, Julian Lage began what he calls a writing sprint as he prepared for a four-day residency at SFJAZZ and the premiere of a new quartet of old collaborators and friends: Lage with bassist Jorge Roeder, drummer Kenny Wollesen, and keyboardist John Medeski. As he thought about their qualities as players and how they might interact, he set a timer for 20 minutes, wrote a tune, recorded it once, and then began again. That is the spirit of Scenes from Above, Lage’s second full-length album with producer Joe Henry and his first with this quartet. Its nine tracks frame a brilliantly open experience, with four players giving and taking space in equal measure as they explore these songs in one space, in real time. By the end of “Something More,” the quartet has instantly found its rapport — a sad and sweet, four-part prayer and shared wish for better days ahead — four dazzling instrumentalists in a room, talking to one another but never actually over one another.

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: Bulky Waste Day provides an opportunity for Wilsonville residents to dispose of large or unusual items that cannot be picked up curbside. Proof of Wilsonville residence is required to participate. There is no charge to dispose waste. Instead, the City asks participants to donate \(cash, check or Venmo\) to Wilsonville Community Sharing, which provides critical social services assistance to local families in need. Donations are collected on site. Upon arrival, vehicles are directed first to the donations area, then to the scales to be weighed, and then to disposal bays. Participants should only bring items that can be removed from vehicles without staff assistance. Bulky Waste Day accepts many items otherwise hard to dispose of, including dishwashers, televisions, refrigerators, computers, monitors, stoves, dryers, water heaters, couches, mattresses, scrap metal, tables and chairs, and clean, untreated wood. All fuel and oils must be emptied from lawn mowers and other gas-powered equipment. The program does not accept construction debris of any type, propane bottles or canisters, paint, batteries, solvents, thinners, household garbage, car tires, or yard debris.
events.title: Bulky Waste Day

events.summary: Project details: Join the Hoyt Arboretum Friends Saturday Crew to help care for the trees and trails at Hoyt Arboretum! With 189 acres and over 6,000 trees along 12 miles of trails, volunteers are incredibly important to maintaining Hoyt Arboretum's tree collection and trail system. This is a great opportunity to learn about and care for rare and unusual trees and plants from around the world. Stewardship crews occur rain or shine, so please come dressed for the weather, including long pants and sturdy, closed-toe shoes. Volunteers should bring water, snacks, and any personal items they need for the day. We provide gloves, tools, training, and parking passes. A reminder email will be sent out a week prior to the event to confirm details. Register Here Meeting location address: 4000 SW Fairview Blvd. Portland, OR 97221 Map to meeting location Parking and meeting location: Volunteers will meet in the maintenance yard behind the Hoyt Arboretum Visitor Center. There are two pay-to-park lots located near the Visitor Center, along with limited free parking along SW Fairview Blvd. Public transit: The MAX Red and Blue Lines drop off at the Washington Park Station and it's about a 15-minute walk uphill via the Overlook Trail to the meeting location. Plan your trip using the TriMet Trip Planner . Volunteers must be 16 years or older: Volunteers between 16 and 17 are welcome to volunteer without an adult, as long as a youth waiver form has been signed by an adult prior to the event. Contact Rowan for more information about this requirement. Location description and accessibility: Volunteers will be working off of established trails and on uneven surfaces. Some bending, lifting, digging, and use of various tools is required. Volunteers are encouraged to select tasks within their abilities and comfort levels. Two single-stall bathrooms and two water fountains are located at the Visitor Center, which may be up to a 15-minute walk from the work site. Questions? Contact Rowan Moreno at rowan@hoytarboretum.org rowan@hoytarboretum.org or 503-823-5453 Thank you for helping to keep Hoyt Arboretum healthy and beautiful! Here are a few tips to get you ready for your stewardship event. Stewardship Crews happen rain or shine. Please dress for the weather and wear long pants with sturdy, close-toed shoes. Bring water, snacks, and any personal items you might need. Tools, gloves, onsite training, and volunteer parking passes are provided. Registration is required for stewardship crews. Hoyt Arboretum is home to some stinging insects, and stings can occur in the park. If you have any allergies, please bring what you need to be safe and let a crew leader know ahead of time. Please stay home if you are experiencing symptoms of any contagious illness. Hoyt Arboretum welcomes groups looking to get out for a stewardship crew, however if your group is larger than five people, please reach out to schedule a private stewardship crew with us. Contact us to request a private group event.

events.summary: Join the Friends of Errol Heights, Portland Parks & Recreation, and Johnson Creek Watershed Council as we gather at Errol Heights Park for a morning of Land Tending! Accessibility: This event may require standing or squatting/kneeling for long periods of time, walking over uneven ground, bending and lifting heavy objects. Bathrooms are available for this event. CLICK HERE TO RSVP Thank you to our funders and partners for supporting watershed health. The Mintkeski Family Fund of Oregon Community Foundation, Portland General Electric, The City of Portland’s Bureau of Environmental Services, Friends of Errol Heights, and Portland Parks and Recreation.

events.summary: Indivisible PDX D3, Portland District 2 Neighbors Indivisible, SEIU, and other community partners are joining forces on October 17th to embrace our right to vote and make our voices heard. We’ll be gathered at the Portland Convention Center Plaza, 834 NE Martin Luther King Jr Boulevard, between 10 am and noon. Join us for live music, short speeches, honk and wave (bring your signs!), protest art, and tabling as we get out the early vote and say it loud: no thrones, no crowns, no kings. At the rally, you can find out more about early voting, election protection, getting big money out of politics, and strike readiness if election results are threatened. And yes, there will be portable restrooms available! We decide who represents us. We decide what comes next. For more than a year, millions of people have come together to reject the idea that power belongs to kings, billionaires, or politicians who believe they are above the people and the law. Now, we are taking the next step, turning people power into voter power. Unlike previous No Kings actions, No Kings: Vote Early, is not purely a protest. Instead, on October 17th, it's a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard. Because no one person gets to decide our leaders before voters do. On October 17th, join us in local events across the country as we get out the early vote and say it loud: no thrones, no crowns, no kings. No Kings: Vote Early events are nonpartisan and are designed to increase participation from all eligible voters. A core principle behind all No Kings events is a commitment to nonviolent action. We expect all participants to seek to de-escalate any potential confrontation with those who disagree with our values and to act lawfully at these events. Weapons of any kind, including those legally permitted, should not be brought to events.

events.summary: Lookout Landscape is an immersive art exhibition by Oregon-based artist and designer David Buckley Borden and a team of collaborators working across forestry, design, and engineering. Inspired by fire lookout towers, trail culture, and backcountry gear, the exhibition invites visitors onto a fabricated “Lookout Trail,” where a series of imaginative scenes—from a trailhead to a weather station, campground, and tool shed—reimagine the visual language of forestry and outdoor culture in the Pacific Northwest. Blending research, humor, and design, the exhibition explores the complex relationships between people and working forests, with wildfire as an underlying thread. As visitors move through the space, they are encouraged to reflect on how forests are shaped, valued, and cared for, and to consider their own connection to these landscapes. Plan your visit and explore the exhibition: worldforestry.org/lookout-landscape

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Skeletons Out of the Closet The annual Spooky Art Show returns to Lavaun's Community Gallery for its third year, this time as “Skeleton's Out of the Closet.” Curated from an open call for submissions, this show features art that is spooky, scary, strange, and out of the ordinary. Alberta Street Gallery member Julia Alora, a lifetime lover of Halloween, has hand-picked this year’s collection of frights and delights from more than 10 local artists. What makes art spooky? Art that focuses on fears, phobias, or disquieting themes. Settings or characters or creatures that are dark, born from night, or upsetting to see. Images that capture the fun and nostalgia of playing in a scary space through a safe lens, reminiscent of horror movies and Halloweens past. Come in for a thrill and a chill, find a new piece to haunt your home, and enjoy beautiful works of art perfect for those who are strange and unusual. Alberta Street Gallery is a friendly and vibrant cooperative gallery of 30 local artists in the heart of the Alberta Arts District in Northeast Portland. In addition to our members’ art, we mount monthly shows that begin on the “Last Thursday” of every month. Our front windows feature new work by two of our member artists, and we curate group shows in Lavaun's Community Gallery, a special exhibition space inside the gallery named for and made possible by gallery member Lavaun Benavidez Heaster, a legally blind collage artist who died in 2020.

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Sergei Rachmaninoff (1873-1943): All-Night Vigil Composed in 1915, Sergei Rachmaninoff’s All-Night Vigil stands as one of the most beautiful choral masterworks ever written—a luminous bridge between ancient Slavic spiritual traditions and late-Romantic expression, with bass notes so low they challenge the limits of the human voice. Drawing deeply from ancient Russian Orthodox chants, Rachmaninoff weaves the timeless melodies of Russian plainsong into works of transcendent beauty. Cappella Romana presents the Vigil as intended, with unadorned Russian chants filling out the Vigil — palette cleansers between Rachmaninoff’s sumptuous courses. This is music that transforms—an outpouring of profound emotional and spiritual vision that finds beauty in darkness. This performance won’t last all night, but you’ll wish it did.
events.title: Sergei Rachmaninoff’s All-Night Vigil

events.summary: The Literary Arts Bookstore & Cafe is excited to welcome author Kelly Grace Thomas to celebrate the release of her memoir-in-verse, Future Tense. Thomas will be joined in conversation by local poet Joy Sullivan. About the book: Reckoning with infertility, adoption, and love under pressure, Kelly Grace Thomas’s Future Tense is a searing memoir-in-verse about a woman’s fight to become a mother while losing her own. Thomas spends three years trying for a child who never arrives. As she struggles with infertility, her mother is dying of Stage IV uterine cancer, and the desire for a child turns urgent—a countdown. As her mother’s health deteriorates, time narrows, pressure builds, and the clock refuses to slow. As her marriage strains and the world remakes itself without her, Thomas refuses to give up. The fertility clinic is the coldest place on earth; still, she keeps going—through years of medical gaslighting, IVF consults, mounting debt, and backhanded blame—finally welcoming her daughter through adoption just months before her mother’s death. Intimate and unflinching, Future Tense interrogates the intertwined joys and griefs of womanhood and motherhood—and how biology can sometimes turn against us. Thomas approaches illness and loss with clarity and care, writing with a generosity that welcomes readers in. Despite their brevity, these poems refuse despair, finding meaning and connection even in the hardest seasons of life.
events.title: Kelly Grace Thomas in conversation with Joy Sullivan

events.summary: Calum Graham: Calum Graham is an internationally acclaimed fingerstyle guitarist, songwriter, and composer whose innovative approach to acoustic guitar has captivated audiences around the world. He began playing guitar at 13, learning from his father, and made history at 17 by winning the 2010 Canadian Fingerstyle Guitar Competition. His early success led to performances at both the Vancouver and London Olympics, launching a career defined by creativity, technical mastery, and a distinctive musical voice. Calum’s sound is a captivating blend of virtuosic fingerstyle guitar, soulful vocals, intricate harmonies, and cinematic arrangements. His music moves effortlessly between intimate, emotionally charged melodies and expansive, richly layered compositions, often drawing on elements of folk, jazz, pop, and contemporary instrumental music. Whether playing solo or with collaborators, he has a remarkable ability to make the guitar sound like an entire ensemble. Since then, Calum has released nine studio albums, collaborated with renowned artists including Don Ross, Antoine Dufour, and Michael Manring, and toured extensively across North America, Australia, and beyond. He is also a member of Tripliciti, a trio with fellow guitar virtuosos Andy McKee and Trevor Gordon Hall. Known for his expressive playing, inventive arrangements, and ability to push the boundaries of contemporary acoustic guitar, Calum brings a rare combination of technical brilliance and genuine emotional depth to every performance.

Based on Susan Hill’s beloved novel, it’s one of the most celebrated ghost stories ever staged: atmospheric, relentless, and the kind of theatrical experience that makes you question every shadow on your way to the car. events.summary: "Marigolds y Memorias" is an original devised production inspired by the traveling carpa tradition, in which humor, music, and storytelling come together in a vibrant theatrical journey. Guided by an elder, a younger generation learns to build an altar, the heart of Día de Muertos, discovering the meaning behind each of its elements, from candles and marigolds to photographs, ofrendas, and cherished recuerdos. Through song, dance, and short theatrical vignettes, the altar gradually takes shape as an act of remembrance and cultural inheritance, inviting audiences to consider how traditions are taught, how memory is kept alive, and what is carried forward when we share rituals across generations.
